## Who is this for?

This is an introductory course on how to use the R programming language.

It is aimed at anyone who has either never used R before or considers themselves a beginner. As the course goes on the topics get more complicated and specialised.

Although there will be some refreshers on basic statistical concepts, this course is about R, not statistics.

## Why use R?

R is an incredibly powerful data analysis tool. Almost any analysis you can dream up can be performed using R. It will do everything from identifying missing data to performing advance machine learning. You can easily create tables and publication ready figures, with far more flexibility and customisation than you could with more standard tools.

R is open source and widely used. The scripts you create to perform your analyses document clearly the steps and decisions you have made. This makes it easy to collaborate on analyses, trace back where any mistakes may have occurred, and ultimately to publish the fruits of your labour. Many journals now insist on you sharing you analysis code; this is good both for transparency and for the advancement of science.

## The structure

The course is **six core weeks**, starting with the basics and building up to reshaping and combining datasets. There are then **two optional bonus weeks** for anyone who wants to go further, one on basic statistical analysis and one on regression.

We will meet once a week for 60-90 minutes where we will work through some interactive teaching together. Each week there will be some exercises to complete after the session to consolidate you learning. These should take you no more than 1 hour to work through (and often will be much quicker). I will send round the my answers to these each week and we will use the first ten minutes of each session to cover any issues that came up.

The course will be dynamically structured around the needs and proficiency of those who attend, however a rough outline is provided below.

The confirmed plan for the upcoming two weeks will be show on the Timetable page, along with the answers to the previous homework exercises and the session recordings.

## The core weeks

# Week 1: Introduction

A guided tour of R studio and how to customise it

R as a fancy calculator

Objects and vectors

# Week 2: More complex object types

Matrices, dataframes and lists

Selecting and changing items in base R

# Week 3: Data importing and packages

Installing and loading packages

Reading data in from CSV and Excel files

Exploring and summarising a new dataset

Spotting outliers and errors, and correcting them safely

# Week 4: The tidyverse

The idea of tidy data (one variable per column, one observation per row)

The pipe (\|\> / %\>%) and why it helps make code readable

The core dplyr verbs: filter, mutate, summarise, group_by

Building conditional columns with case_when

# Week 5: Visualisation with ggplot2

The grammar of graphics: data → aesthetics → geoms

Common "geoms" (point, line, boxplot) and mapping colour, fill and group

Titles, labels and themes to get to a publication-ready figure

# Week 6: Reshaping and joining data

Moving between wide and long formats with pivot_longer and pivot_wider

Joining tables that share a key, and the difference between left, right, inner and full joins

## The bonus weeks

These two weeks are optional. This course is about R rather than statistics, so if you already have the analysis skills you need, the first six weeks are a complete introduction on their own. The bonus weeks are here for anyone who wants to see how the tools carry over into a statistical analysis.

# Bonus week: Statistical analysis

Choosing a test to match your question

t-tests (one-sample, two-sample and paired), and their non-parametric equivalents

Comparing more than two groups with ANOVA

Chi-squared and Fisher's exact tests for counts

Correlation

There is a fuller, code-free explanation of the ideas behind these tests on the [Statistics refresher](stats_explained.qmd) page.

# Bonus week: Regression

Fitting a linear model with lm() and reading its output

Interpreting coefficients, confidence intervals and p-values

Adding categorical predictors

Tidying model output with the broom package
